question.text: A PMS equity portfolio with Sharpe Ratio of 1.5 is:

answer.text: Good to excellent (>1 is typically good)

explanation.text: The Logic: The Sharpe Ratio measures excess return per unit of total risk (standard deviation). A higher Sharpe Ratio indicates better risk-adjusted performance. As a common industry rule of thumb, a Sharpe Ratio above 1 is generally regarded as good and a sustained Sharpe Ratio around 1.5 is regarded as good-to-excellent on a risk-adjusted basis. The Trap: Labelling a 1.5 Sharpe portfolio "poor," "average," or "terrible" inverts the risk-adjusted return interpretation. Comparisons should always be made versus a relevant benchmark Sharpe over the same period. Note: The Portfolio Managers (NISM-Series-XXI-B) workbook explains Sharpe Ratio calculation and states that higher Sharpe Ratios indicate better risk-adjusted performance, but it does not endorse the specific absolute thresholds (>1 good, ~1.5 good-to-excellent). Those benchmarks are general industry conventions used here only as descriptive framing.
